results.blind_working: ΔΦ per turn = 4 − 1 = 3 mWb. |e| = NΔΦ/Δt = 100 × 3×10⁻³ / 0.02 = 15 V.
dΦ/dt = (6t − 2)×10⁻³ Wb/s, which is 10×10⁻³ Wb/s at t = 2 s. |e| = N dΦ/dt = 20 × 0.01 = 0.2 V.
Initial flux per turn = BA = 0.4 × 0.05 = 0.02 Wb; final flux = 0 (plane parallel to field). |e| = NΔΦ/Δt = 200 × 0.02 / 0.5 = 8 V.
A coil at rest in a steady field has no change in flux, so no emf is induced: A is false. Induced emf depends on the rate of change of flux, not on the flux itself: R is true.
e = −dΦ/dt = Φ₀ω sin ωt, which is zero when cos ωt = ±1, i.e. when flux is maximum: I is correct. An emf is induced in an open coil even though no current flows: II is correct.
ε = Blv = 0.5 × 0.4 × 5 = 1 V; P = ε²/R = 1²/2 = 0.5 W, which the agent must supply at constant speed
A: moving rod gives Blv (III). B: rod rotating about one end gives ½Bωl² (I). C: induced charge is NΔΦ/R (IV). D: power is ε²/R (II).

A true: the approaching N pole is opposed, so the near face is N. B false: a receding magnet is attracted, not repelled. C true: Lenz's law follows from energy conservation. D false: F = B²l²v/R, so F ∝ v, not v². E true: P = ε²/R ∝ cos²t, which is never negative. Correct set is A, C, E.
For a long solenoid L = mu0 N^2 A / l, so L is proportional to N^2. Doubling N gives 4 x 2 mH = 8 mH.
In parallel both inductors have the same emf, so L1 dI1/dt = L2 dI2/dt. The rates are inversely proportional to L, i.e. 6:2 = 3:1. Splitting 8 A/s in that ratio gives 6 A/s for the 2 mH inductor.
L = mu0 n^2 pi r^2 l (III); M = mu0 n1 n2 pi r1^2 l (IV); energy stored = (1/2) L I^2 (I); energy density = B^2/(2 mu0) (II).

A is false: L depends on geometry and the medium, not on the current. B is true: a core of relative permeability mu_r multiplies L by mu_r. C is true: M12 = M21 by reciprocity. D is false: k is at most 1. E is true: in series the current is the same, so each emf is L dI/dt and the emfs are proportional to L.
An ammeter reads the rms value, so I0 = √2 × 5 = 7.07 A.
The half-cycle mean is 2I0/π = 14, so I0 = 14π/2 = 7 × 22/7 = 22 A. Then Irms = 22/√2 ≈ 15.6 A.
For the square wave, I² = I0² at all times, so Irms = I0 and A is true. R is also true, but it concerns the sinusoidal case and does not explain A.
Statement I: the mean over a full cycle is 0, so I is false. Statement II: rms/mean = (I0/√2)/(2I0/π) = π/(2√2) ≈ 1.11. The value 0.90 is mean/rms, so II is false.
For a pure capacitor, i = C dv/dt. With v = V0 sin ωt, i = ωCV0 cos ωt, so the current leads the voltage by π/2.
XL = ωL (IV). XC = 1/(ωC) (III). Z = √(R² + (XL − XC)²) (I). I0 = V0/Z (II).

A is true because XL is proportional to f. B is true because XC → ∞ as ω → 0. C is false because the voltages add as phasors, not arithmetically. D is false because an ideal inductor is a short circuit for DC. E is true because XC is proportional to 1/f.
At resonance X_L = X_C, so Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2) = R.

At resonance V_L = V_C, they are opposite in phase and cancel, so the source supplies only V_R. V_L = I·X_L = Q·V can then exceed V when Q > 1. Both statements are true; R is taken as the explanation, though it is arguable since the size of V_L depends on Q.

Below resonance X_C > X_L, so the circuit is capacitive and current leads voltage: I is correct. Resonant frequency 1/sqrt(LC) does not depend on R, and higher R makes resonance broader, not sharper: II is incorrect.
In a pure inductor the current lags the voltage by 90°, so cos φ = 0 and P = V_rms·I_rms·cos 90° = 0.
cos φ = 0.6 gives sin φ = 0.8. Wattless current = I_rms·sin φ = 10 × 0.8 = 8 A.

A: pure inductor has φ = 90°, so pf = 0 (III). B: at resonance the circuit is purely resistive, so pf = 1 (I). C: Z = √(30² + 40²) = 50 Ω, so pf = 30/50 = 0.6 (II). D: with R = X_L, φ = 45°, so pf ≈ 0.707 (IV).

A is true: cos φ = R/Z. B is true: only the resistor dissipates power, so P = I_rms²R. C is false: a low pf needs a larger current for the same power. D is true: capacitors offset inductive loads and raise the pf. E is false: the wattless component is 90° out of phase with the voltage. Correct set: A, B, D.
e = NBAω sin ωt, where ωt is the angle between the field and the coil plane's normal. The emf is maximum when the coil plane is parallel to B, because the flux is then zero but changing fastest.
ε0 ∝ Bω, so (B/2)(2ω) gives ε0 unchanged. The frequency f = ω/2π doubles to 2f.
A is true because ε0 = NBAω is proportional to ω. R is true because the emf frequency equals the rotation frequency. R concerns frequency, not peak value, so it does not explain A.
I is true: emf is zero when flux linkage is maximum. II: sin ωt = 1/2 gives |cos ωt| = √3/2, so flux linkage NBA cos ωt = (√3/2)NBA. Both statements are correct.
A transformer works by mutual induction from a changing flux, so the secondary EMF has the same frequency as the primary. Voltage, current and number of turns all change in a step-up transformer.
Output power = 11 × 4 = 44 W. Input power = 44 / 0.8 = 55 W. Primary current Ip = 55 / 220 = 0.25 A.
At 20 kV the line current is I = 100 kW / 20 kV = 5 A. Loss = I²R = 25 × 5 = 125 W. Check: at 10 kV, I = 10 A and loss = 500 W, so doubling the voltage cuts the loss by a factor of 4.

Flux leakage is reduced by winding the coils one over the other (A-IV). Copper loss is reduced by thick wires (B-II). Eddy-current loss is reduced by a laminated core (C-I). Hysteresis loss is reduced by a soft-iron core with a narrow loop (D-III).

A is true: voltage rises and current falls. B is false: steady DC gives no changing flux, so no induced EMF. C is true: frequency is unchanged. D is false: an ideal transformer conserves power. E is true: lower line current reduces I²R losses. Correct set is A, C and E.
